summary.text: Case 1, an 80-year-old female, underwent total arch replacement for Stanford type A acute aortic dissection. Abdominal pain prompted evaluation alongside inflammatory markers. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 11.9 ×10³/μL and CRP 18.6 mg/dL. Gallstones were absent and the case was acalculous. Contrast CT showed reduced gallbladder-wall enhancement. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurred 9 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of same day, operative time 80 min and blood loss 15 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as diffuse on the dorsal side, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed necrosis from mucosa to outer fat-rich subserosal layer at leakage sites. No apparent RAS or perioperative cholecystectomy-related complications were reported. The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.

summary.text: Case 2, a 75-year-old female, had Stanford type A acute aortic dissection and cerebral infarction, and underwent total arch replacement for the dissection. Abdominal pain was explicitly absent; inflammatory-marker evaluation prompted imaging. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 17.1 ×10³/μL and CRP 12.9 mg/dL. Gallstones were absent and the case was acalculous. Contrast CT showed reduced gallbladder-wall enhancement. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurred 10 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of 5 days later, operative time 116 min and blood loss 12 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as neck, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed necrosis from mucosa to outer fat-rich subserosal layer at leakage sites. No apparent RAS or perioperative cholecystectomy-related complications were reported. The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.

summary.text: Case 4, a 79-year-old male, underwent endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. Abdominal pain was explicitly absent; inflammatory-marker evaluation prompted imaging. Pre-cholecystectomy WBC was 21.1 ×10³/μL and CRP 32.5 mg/dL. Gallstones were absent and the case was acalculous. Contrast CT showed reduced gallbladder-wall enhancement. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurred 5 days after the cardiovascular operation, with an estimated onset-to-operation interval of same day, operative time 125 min and blood loss 10 mL. The bile-leak distribution was recorded as diffuse, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed markedly thinned wall/full-thickness necrosis with layer structure difficult to evaluate. No apparent RAS or perioperative cholecystectomy-related complications were reported. The patient survived the reported postoperative course; discharge date and longer-term follow-up were not supplied. Preoperative CT also showed significant aortic calcifications and stenosis/mural thrombi in celiac or common hepatic arteries, without case-specific artery identification.

The bile-leak distribution was recorded as neck to body, without overt perforation. Histology supported gangrenous cholecystitis and showed multiple ulcers from mucosal to subserosal layer. Severe heart failure/massive pleural effusion motivated open surgery; postoperative sputum retention required tracheostomy (gradeIIIb). Perioperative hypoperfusion/redistributed splanchnic flow is an author hypothesis, not confirmed NOMI or a documented hemodynamic measurement in any case.
The five patient rows are individually extractable. No explicit same-patient prior-publication link identified; literature cases and institutional larger cohorts remain background.
No individual medications, doses, discharge dates or longitudinal follow-up are reported. Series symptom wording does not establish fever in every pain-negative patient.

Figure 3 caption refers to contrast loss on CT in each case, whereas Case 3 is explicitly the noncontrast CT/MRI patient; no contrast-enhanced CT finding is newly assigned to Case 3 from that generic caption.

Introductory series wording describes development 3–10 days after primary surgery, but Table 1 explicitly labels those case-specific intervals as primary surgery to cholecystectomy and separately gives estimated onset-to-cholecystectomy intervals. No individual onset date is calculated or silently equated with the operative interval.
